### Environment

ESLint Playground

### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

### Playground Code
```js
/*eslint no-unreachable: "error"*/

import foo from 'foo';

console.log('bar');

throw new Error();

import baz from 'baz';
```

### ESLint Configuration 
<details> 
 <summary> Tap to see full config </summary> 

```js
import { defineConfig } from "eslint/config";

export default defineConfig([
    {
        "languageOptions": {
            "sourceType": "module"
        }
    }
]);
```
 </details>

### ESLint Output
```
9:1 Unreachable code. (no-unreachable)
```


### What did you expect to happen?

no lint report

### What actually happened?

9:1 Unreachable code. (no-unreachable)

### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#

### Participation

- [ ] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [x] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [ ] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

Wasn't sure whether to report this as a bug against the code path analysis itself. The code explorer shows the import as unreachable due to interpreting it as ordinary source code, rather than being hoisted for the purposes of control flow ([link](https://explorer.eslint.org/#eslint-explorer=v2.-ZWxlbWVudHM8L3NwYW4--XG4gICAgICAgIDx0aXRsZT5IVE1MPC90aXRsZT5cbiAgICA8L2hlYWQ-XG4gICAgPGJvZHk-XG4gICAgICAgIDxwPlRleHQ8L3A-)). This seems kind of wrong to me? Imports really aren't part of the top-level execution code path at all; they're more like their own thing that happens before the top-level execution.

items.body:
### Environment

Node version: v24.14.1
npm version: 11.11.1
Local ESLint version: v10.7.0
Global ESLint version: v10.7.0
Operating System: Window 11


### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

<details>
<summary>Configuration</summary>

```js
export default [
    {
        files: ["**/*.js"],
        languageOptions: { ecmaVersion: 'lastest', sourceType: "module" },
        rules: { "no-var": "error" }
    }
];
```
</details>

```js
function f() {
    try {
        throw new Error("boom");
    } catch (e) {
        var e = e || new Error("unknown");
        console.log(e.message);
    }
}
f();
```
Running `npx eslint --fix c.js`.

### What did you expect to happen?

The declaration should not be autofixed. Per the spec, a `var` may
redeclare a catch clause parameter (B.3.4), but a `let` with the same
name is a SyntaxError. This is the same category as #11830 (`var let;`),
where autofix was disabled because the result would not parse.

### What actually happened?

The declaration was autofixed to `let`:

```js
    } catch (e) {
        let e = e || new Error("unknown");
```

Before the fix, the code runs and prints `boom`. After the fix, it does
not parse at all:

SyntaxError: Identifier 'e' has already been declared

Notably, ESLint itself reports a parsing error on its own output when
running `--fix`:

5:13 error Parsing error: Identifier 'e' has already been declared

Since this is a parse failure rather than a runtime change, the entire
script fails to load, taking any other code in the same file with it.

### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

`isRedeclared` checks `variable.defs.length >= 2`, but the catch
parameter and the `var` resolve to separate variables in the scope
analysis, so the redeclaration is not detected. The equivalent case with
a *function* parameter is handled correctly and is not autofixed:

```js
function f(e) { var e = e || "fallback"; }  // correctly not fixed
function f() { try {} catch (e) { var e = e || "fallback"; } }  // fixed -> SyntaxError
```

This pattern (`catch (e) { var e = e || ... }`) shows up in older
cross-browser error handling code, so it can surface when running
`--fix` over a legacy codebase.

I am willing to submit a pull request to fix this.

labels.description: There is consensus among the team that this change meets the criteria for inclusion
labels.name: accepted

items.title: Bug: `no-var` autofix produces a SyntaxError when a `var` redeclares the catch clause parameter

items.body:
### Environment

Node version: v24.14.1
npm version: 11.11.0
Local ESLint version: v10.7.0
Global ESLint version: v10.7.0 
Operating System: Window 11


### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

<details>
<summary>Configuration</summary>

```js
export default [
    {
        files: ["**/*.js"],
        languageOptions: { ecmaVersion: 'latest', sourceType: "module" },
        rules: { "no-var": "error" }
    }
];
```
</details>

```js
function wrap() {
    foo();
    var a = 1;
    function foo() { console.log(a); }
}
wrap();
```
Running `npx eslint --fix t.js`.

### What did you expect to happen?

The declaration should not be autofixed, because `foo` is hoisted and is
called before `var a = 1` is evaluated. Converting to `let` moves that
read into the TDZ.

This looks like the same class of issue as #20209, which was addressed in
#20464 by adding `hasReferenceBeforeDeclaration`. That fix covers cases
where the reference appears textually before the declaration, e.g.:

```js
function test() { console.log(x); var x = 1; }  // correctly not fixed
```

The case above is the same hazard, but the reference sits textually
*after* the declaration, inside a hoisted function declaration that is
invoked before it.

### What actually happened?

The declaration was autofixed to `let`:

```js
function wrap() {
    foo();
    let a = 1;
    function foo() { console.log(a); }
}
wrap();
```

Before the fix, the code runs and prints `undefined`. After the fix, it
throws:
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'a' before initialization



### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#

### Participation

- [ ] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

`hasReferenceBeforeDeclaration` compares source positions:

```js
return !reference.init && referenceStart < declarationStart;
```

Because function declarations are hoisted, the position of a reference
inside the function body does not reflect when that reference is
evaluated. Moving the function declaration above the `var` makes the
existing check catch it, so the behavior depends on where the function
is placed:

```js
function wrap() { function foo() { a } var a = 1; foo() }  // not fixed
function wrap() { foo(); var a = 1; function foo() { a } } // fixed -> throws
```

I understand fully resolving this in general would require call-graph
reachability analysis, which may be out of scope. Reporting in case the
narrower pattern (a function declaration in the same scope, called before
the declaration) is worth handling.

labels.description: There is consensus among the team that this change meets the criteria for inclusion
labels.name: accepted

### Environment

Node version: v22.19.0
npm version: 11.17.0
Local ESLint version: v10.8.0
Global ESLint version: N/A
Operating System: macOS Darwin 25.5.0

### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

**Configuration**

```js
export default [
  {
    rules: {
      "no-unused-labels": "error"
    }
  }
];
```

**Code**

```js
function foo() {}
foo()
LABEL: [1, 2, 3].forEach(x => x)
```

Run ESLint with `--fix` flag or apply the autofix from the editor.

### What did you expect to happen?

No autofix should be applied, because removing the label would create an ASI hazard — the two statements would be merged into one by the JS engine.

### What actually happened?

The autofix removes `LABEL: ` and produces:

```js
function foo() {}
foo()
[1, 2, 3].forEach(x => x)
```

This is parsed as a **single statement**:

```js
foo()[1, 2, 3].forEach(x => x)
```

which is semantically completely different from the original code.

The same issue occurs when the label body starts with `(`, `/`, `+`, `-`, or a template literal (`` ` ``).

### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#eyJ0ZXh0IjoiLyogZXNsaW50IG5vLXVudXNlZC1sYWJlbHM6IFwiZXJyb3JcIiAqL1xuZnVuY3Rpb24gZm9vKCkge31cbmZvbygpXG5MQUJFTDogWzEsIDIsIDNdLmZvckVhY2goeCA9PiB4KSIsIm9wdGlvbnMiOnsicnVsZXMiOnsibm8tdW51c2VkLWxhYmVscyI6WyJlcnJvciJdfSwibGFuZ3VhZ2VPcHRpb25zIjp7InBhcnNlck9wdGlvbnMiOnsiZWNtYUZlYXR1cmVzIjp7fX19fX0=

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [x] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [ ] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

Issue #16988 / PR #17314 previously added a guard to prevent autofix when removing the label would turn the body into a directive (string literal). However, isFixable() still does not check for ASI hazards caused by tokens like [, (, `, /, +, -.

The no-console rule already handles this pattern correctly via its maybeAsiHazard() function (see lib/rules/no-console.js).

labels.name: accepted

items.body:
### Environment

ESLint Playground

### What parser are you using?

Default (Espree)

### What did you do?

<!-- The configuration and code have been saved to clipboard. Please paste them here 👇🏻 -->
```js
// Case 1: `get` in the target object, not in the property descriptor
Object.defineProperty({ get(key) {} }, "name", { value: 1 });
Object.create({ foo: { get(key) {} } }, { bar: { value: 1 } });

// Case 2: `Object` is shadowed, not the global `Object`
function f(Object) {
    Object.defineProperty({}, "k", { get() {} });
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

No errors should be reported in either case.

Case 1: The get method is in the target object argument, not in the property descriptor argument, so it is not a getter.
Case 2: Object is shadowed by a function parameter, so this is not a call to the global `Object.defineProperty` and the rule should not apply.

Note that the similar rule `no-setter-return` handles both cases correctly with its `isArgumentOfGlobalMethodCall()` and `isPropertyDescriptor()` helper functions: https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/d08629382b0a6aaa042823b796e5100e60053b54/lib/rules/no-setter-return.js#L28-L104

### What actually happened?

<!-- The lint output for what actually happened has been copied in What did you do? field above. -->
Errors are reported in all three places:

`2:25 Expected to return a value in method 'get'.`
`3:24 Expected to return a value in method 'get'.`
`7:38 Expected to return a value in method 'get'.`

### Link to Minimal Reproducible Example

https://eslint.org/play/#

### Participation

- [x] I am willing to submit a pull request for this issue.

### AI acknowledgment

- [ ] I did not use AI to generate this issue report.
- [x] (If the above is not checked) I have reviewed the AI-generated content before submitting.

### Additional comments

Since both false positives come from the same check in `getter-return`, I think a single PR can fix both — happy to split it if the team prefers.

I'd like to fix them by applying the same validation that `no-setter-return`'s helpers (`isArgumentOfGlobalMethodCall()` / `isPropertyDescriptor()`) already perform: **checking the argument position and verifying that the call references the global object.**

One question about the implementation: `accessor-pairs` also has nearly identical logic,
https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/eddbad60158d8cda86830fbe934a9d2282273b32/lib/rules/accessor-pairs.js#L90-L138
so this fix would mean a third copy of the same helpers. Would it be better to move them into `ast-utils.js` for reuse, or should I just duplicate them in `getter-return` for now and leave the extraction for a follow-up?

labels.description: There is consensus among the team that this change meets the criteria for inclusion
labels.name: accepted
